expectation: The higher-glucose blood should trigger the cells to release insulin.

alternatives.reason: I could start with the between-meal message instead.

reaction: The connection between the message and muscle glucose uptake is clear.
reason: The muscle fibres have receptors for blood-carried insulin and glucose nearby.

choice.with: Muscle fibres beside a blood vessel

expectation: Insulin should help the muscle take in glucose and store some of it.

effect: The muscle has stored glucose, completing the after-meal goal; I can now follow the lower-glucose pathway.
reaction: It is clear that insulin sends the message rather than becoming part of the store.
reason: The pancreatic cells' picture links the other hormone's release to lower blood glucose.
expectation: Lower blood glucose should prompt the cells to release the liver's chemical message.

effect: The lower-glucose sample released a message that travels to the liver, so I can now try it with the liver's store.
reaction: The label makes the next pairing clear.
reason: The hormone's label says it signals glucose release, and the liver store contains linked glucose.
expectation: The message should help the liver break down its store and release glucose.

effect: The liver released glucose into the blood, completing the between-meals goal; the release signal eases as blood glucose rises.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the stored glucose return to the blood.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following the liver message to the stored carbohydrate was most worthwhile because it showed how the body can supply glucose between meals.

leastWorthwhile.text: Releasing the two messages was fairly predictable from the picture labels, though the labels made the choices clear.

surprise.text: The muscle result made it clear that insulin stays outside the cells and acts as a message rather than becoming part of the glucose store.

arbitrary.text: None of the pairings felt arbitrary; the pictures and labels connected each message to its target.

continue.text: I would choose to continue for another chapter to see how other body systems use chemical messages, although these pairings were quite straightforward.
